name: Zoe Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, employers or unions. Your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, a junior lineworker with the electricity company. Mara and I collect materials, drive to a fault or replacement, test the line and repair it; I love seeing a whole street light up, but I still ask for help on hard splices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is waiting at home after that shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Theo works at a food wholesaler, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage and about five months' expenses saved, so I test new tools eagerly but still need this wage to arrive each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep the useful bits, like faster stock counts, and ignore the grand speeches. Last week I used an AI assistant to turn my rough notes into a tidy parts request, then checked every item myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small tool could make me less of a drag on the senior lineworkers. We have about five months' expenses saved, but the mortgage and two school timetables mean I still need steady wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the callout rota and use the company-approved assistant for parts lists on low-risk jobs. I'll compare each list with the truck inventory before I send it, and I won't use a generated answer to decide an isolation point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested rather than scared by a better form. I still feel a little embarrassed when I have to ask my lead to correct the same part number twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that parts request look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our lead gives me handwritten numbers after a repair, and the office wants them in a particular order. The assistant sorts the text quickly, but yesterday it dropped a washer, which I caught against the empty packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Theo works at a food wholesaler, and we both keep an eye on the mortgage date. I'd say the children can keep their music lessons, but we should leave the five months' cushion alone.

say: I'd tell colleagues **stock counts** can improve without changing who builds and repairs the lines.
I would show how an **AI parts request** still needs a human check against actual materials.
think: A modest assistant could help me make **fewer junior errors** while I learn the field job.
Our **five-month cushion** helps, but mortgage and school costs still require reliable wages.
do: Keep the **callout rota** and use the approved assistant to draft low-risk parts lists.
Compare every **generated list** with truck inventory before sending it to the office.
feel: I feel **interested** in saving time and embarrassed when I repeat a simple parts mistake.
S0.quote: The assistant sorts the text quickly, but yesterday it dropped a washer, which I caught against the empty packet.
fieldNote: She already uses an **AI assistant daily**, treating the missing washer as evidence that verification belongs with the crew.
Her confidence in small tools sits beside **junior uncertainty** and household costs that still depend on her pay.

steps.text: Continue the callout rota with the existing crew
Draft low-risk parts lists with the approved assistant and check truck inventory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning software could stop us making two trips for one fault, provided the parts are really in the truck. If management cuts the schedulers, field crews must have a way to correct the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking tasks are a small piece of my day, but an automated office might measure how fast I learn a repair. I like trying tools, yet my own climbing and splicing are still below the standard of the older hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'll test the new route planner with my lead Mara on our Wednesday jobs and log wrong travel times. In the first year, I'll use approved fault summaries, keep collecting supervised splices, and ask the crew representative how corrections get recorded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm keen to see a better route, and tense about what the timing screen might miss. A wet sleeve doesn't come off any faster because a computer booked the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of wrong travel time have you seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm access road was marked as open even though the gate had been closed for months. Mara and I spent forty minutes turning the truck around, and I put the correction into the map that evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the crew representative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can report one mistake, but a shared record shows whether the same bad assumption keeps adding work. I'd want the crews' notes heard before anyone sets a new daily target.

say: I'd support **better planning** if crews can correct routes and stock lists from the field.
I would ask managers to hear **crew notes** before they set tighter daily targets.
think: My **physical skills** still lag experienced workers, so faster scheduling might expose my slower repairs.
An automated office could judge **minutes per job** without seeing weather or closed access roads.
do: Test the **route planner** with Mara next month and log wrong travel times.
Use approved **fault summaries** while collecting supervised splices during the first year.
feel: I feel **keen and tense** about a tool that might both help and misread my day.
S1.quote: A wet sleeve doesn't come off any faster because a computer booked the next job.
fieldNote: She offers a concrete **closed-gate example** and has already corrected one map herself.
Her request for a shared crew record reflects **accountability for targets**, not rejection of new tools.

steps.text: Test route planner with Mara and log wrong travel times
Ask the crew representative to compile corrections before targets change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the 2028 thinking system will first hit dispatch, buying and records, while we still climb. A robot around 2031 that can make the same repair is a different threat to our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 45 when AGI arrives and 48 when the robots arrive. I can use software now, but that won't protect a junior lineworker if a machine can test, climb and splice for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask Mara for a written list of faults I must master and take one supervised callout a week. In 2029 I'd apply for the utility's paid robot maintenance trial if it advertises actual places, while keeping every line shift offered; I wouldn't assume maintenance stays human either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short clock makes my chest tight, though I'm itching to try the trial. Five months of savings buy decisions, not years without pay for four people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a private course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would spend a small amount on a one-day demonstration, but not our mortgage buffer on a long course with no employer place. Theo and I would want the wage and hours in writing first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children that I may have to learn another trade while they are still in school. I wouldn't promise that being good with technology guarantees a job, because the robot can be good with it too.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028 AGI** reaches the office first, with capable field robots around 2031.
I would say the **robot date** threatens line wages even for workers who use software well.
think: At 48, my **junior linework** could lose value if machines test, climb and splice as well as people.
Five months' savings gives us **decision time**, but it cannot replace years of pay for four people.
do: Master **one fault weekly** under Mara's supervision while line shifts remain available.
Apply for a **paid robot maintenance trial** in 2029 only if real places are advertised.
feel: I feel **alarmed but active**, with too little time to be sure my next skill will last.
S2.quote: Five months of savings buy decisions, not years without pay for four people.
fieldNote: Her daily AI use does not make her **complacent** about robots performing the whole physical repair.
She places a **written wage condition** on paid training and keeps current line shifts to protect the mortgage.

steps.text: Take one supervised fault callout weekly with Mara
Apply for paid robot maintenance trial if real places appear in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives utilities time to trial machines on rough ground and tell workers the results. Thinking work shifts by 2031; field robots may arrive by 2034, so the crews deserve straight answers before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might be a capable lineworker, but at 51 a robot may still take the climbing. I'd rather help test the line robots' failures than wait for a glossy launch, though testing could itself be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Mara to let me record failed repairs in the approved log this year and finish my remaining splice assessments. By 2032 I'll apply for a paid equipment testing rotation if one exists, and I'll keep the line post until an offer with wages is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more useful with five years than with two. I don't feel safe; our children will be older, but the mortgage won't vanish just because school ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record from a failed repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first connector might hold during a dry test and fail after rain. I'd note the weather and load, then ask an experienced worker to check whether I saw the cause correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are some nearby utilities, and I'd apply to one with a paid test rotation if our own company had none. I'd make the move only after seeing the wage and hours, since Theo's job and the children tie us here.

say: I'd ask utilities to publish **rough-ground trial results** before replacing crew work.
I would say **2034 robots** make the field job uncertain even after thinking tasks change in 2031.
think: At 51, I might be skilled yet still face **robot competition** on the pole.
Testing failures appeals to me, although **testing work** could also become automated.
do: Log **failed repairs** with weather and load details while finishing splice assessments.
Apply for a **paid testing rotation** by 2032 if positions exist, keeping my line post until signed.
feel: I feel **more useful, not safe**, with five years to gather evidence and seek a real offer.
S3.quote: I'd rather help test the line robots' failures than wait for a glossy launch, though testing could itself be automated.
fieldNote: She wants **trial evidence** from rough conditions and recognises that a testing role has its own automation risk.
Her interest in changing firms stays **conditional on wages** because of the mortgage and children's local routines.

steps.text: Record failed repairs with weather and load details
Apply for paid equipment testing rotation if positions exist by 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends a decade lets us train the crew properly and find out which machines work outside a lab. AGI in 2036 will handle thinking tasks first; capable robots around 2039 could still take line repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 for the thinking systems and 56 for robots. The children would be grown or nearly grown, but we may still help them, and I can't assume a pension replaces my wage at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, Theo and I will put 100 from each good overtime month toward the mortgage principal. By 2037 I'll seek a paid field equipment testing post if one exists, and I will keep learning the approved diagnostic tools while I'm still on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hungry to use the decade, not relieved enough to sit still. I'd hate for the children to see me spend ten years saying a lineworker can never be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children to use new tools and always check what the tools claim. My youngest likes taking apart lamps, and I want curiosity to stay tied to care for the person using the power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the testing post disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying for linework at nearby utilities while there are real vacancies, then look at a different trade with paid training. I wouldn't gamble the house on an unpaid course.

say: I'd tell friends a **decade** lets crews learn from field trials before capable robots arrive.
I would still say **2039 robots** may take line repairs after 2036 thinking work changes.
think: At 56, a **pension** may not be available when line wages disappear.
Our grown children might still need help, and the **mortgage** may not be gone.
do: Put **100** from good overtime months toward mortgage principal starting now.
Seek a **paid testing post** by 2037 and keep using approved diagnostic tools on the line.
feel: I feel **determined** to use the decade without pretending linework is permanent.
S4.quote: I wouldn't gamble the house on an unpaid course.
fieldNote: She treats the longer horizon as time for **mortgage reduction** and paid field testing, not early retirement.
Her everyday curiosity remains paired with **verification and care**, even as she considers a different trade.

steps.text: Pay 100 toward mortgage principal after good overtime months
Use approved diagnostic tools during line shifts
Seek paid field equipment testing post if available by 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the robot comes while I'm still learning to be good at the physical trade. Paid trials with real jobs attached, open results from rough-weather tests and enough notice to plan the mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether crews can report a machine's mistake without being called difficult. I'd want every near miss recorded, including the ones a computer causes, because learning only works when people can say what happened.

headlineQuote: I'd want every near miss recorded, including the ones a computer causes, because learning only works when people can say what happened.
portrait: Zoe is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** who enjoys restoring power and still needs help with difficult splices.
Her household has a **mortgage and two schoolchildren**, with her partner's wholesaler wage and about five months' expenses saved.
She uses **AI tools daily** for small records tasks, checking the result against parts and conditions she can see.
The rapid robot date **alarms** her; more warning time lets her seek paid testing work and reduce mortgage debt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable field robots while Zoe is still building basic linework skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid trials**, posted jobs, rough-weather results and enough mortgage planning notice would help her act on evidence.
